one_liner: Zero-copy, schema-compiled binary format for Go/TinyGo and WASM; own benchmark: 5-18x faster than FlatBuffers' Go implementation.
what_it_does: Karmem compiles a .km schema (enums, fixed-layout inline structs, append-only tables) into Go/TinyGo, C, Zig, AssemblyScript, Swift, Odin and C# code, so a WASM host and guests written in different languages can all read one encoded buffer. The generated API has three paths: WriteAsRoot encodes a native struct into a Writer, generated Viewers read fields in place from the buffer, and ReadAsRoot decodes into an existing struct that you reuse across messages. It is not wire- or schema-compatible with FlatBuffers, so switching means rewriting schemas and call sites.
how_it_is_fast: Layouts are fixed when the schema is compiled. A table is a uint32 size header followed by fields at constant offsets, with no FlatBuffers-style vtable, so reading a field costs one comparison against the table size plus an unsafe load at a constant offset. Arrays come back as native Go slices built over the buffer from hand-made slice headers, so a loop over them is plain indexing; FlatBuffers Go's Path(&obj, j) does a vtable lookup and a vector dereference for every element. In the README's raw-struct comparison this read loop takes 160 µs against 154 µs for summing a plain Go struct. Object-API decode copies into the destination's existing slices and strings and grows them only when they are too short (0 allocs/op natively, against 110k for FlatBuffers' UnPackTo, which makes fresh slices and pointer structs). Encoding is one pass of typed unsafe stores and memcpy into a preallocated buffer, with no endianness conversion.
when_to_use: A TinyGo or Go WASM module that exchanges structured data with a host or with other guests written in Zig, C, AssemblyScript or Odin, where everyone reads one encoded buffer in place.
Hot loops that repeatedly read a few fields or numeric arrays (e.g. Vec3 paths) out of large messages: Viewers hand back native slices over the buffer, with no per-element accessor calls.
Go code that decodes many messages of the same type into one reused destination struct (e.g. from a sync.Pool) and wants 0 allocations per decode natively.
Schemas made mostly of fixed-size numerics and bounded arrays ([N]T, [<N]T) that only ever add fields, with little-endian machines on both ends.
when_not_to_use: C++ codebases: there is no C++ generator, the C target is a C99 header that relies on GCC/Clang packed attributes, and nobody benchmarked FlatBuffers' C++ path against it.

Untrusted input: a malformed offset silently yields zero/default values instead of an error, and the README warns that shared offsets let a small message expand into large arrays under the Object API. The only mitigation offered is to use limited arrays and avoid the Object API.

Schemas that need unions, optional/nullable fields, arrays of strings, tables or arrays, field removal, or a JavaScript/TypeScript generator. None of these is supported, and the unions (#25) and array-of-strings (#98) issues are still open.

Projects that need a stable API or upstream fixes. The README says the API is unstable, the last code change was in Sep 2022, and the data-corruption report #102 has no reply. The package also panics at init on big-endian targets.

Choosing it for native Go speed on this evidence alone. The only comparison is the project's own benchmark against FlatBuffers' Go object API with a similar but not identical schema, and a request for an independent comparison (#31) was never resolved.

integration.dependencies: Go runtime package (karmem.org/golang): stdlib only (errors, unsafe). The code generator (karmem.org/cmd/karmem) needs golang.org/x/crypto for blake2b packet IDs. Each other target needs its runtime file (c/karmem.h, zig/karmem.zig, assemblyscript/karmem.ts, swift, odin, dotnet).
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.18 (go.mod; the generated code uses unsafe.Add). The README lists Go 1.19 / TinyGo 0.25.0, and CI used Go 1.18.4/1.19 and TinyGo 0.24.0. Other targets: Zig 0.10, AssemblyScript 0.20.16, Swift/SwiftWasm 5.7, .NET 7, C via Emscripten.
integration.platforms: Little-endian 32- or 64-bit only (the package panics at init otherwise). Packed layouts put fields at unaligned offsets. Benchmarked on Apple M1 (native Go and wasm32-wasi under wazero); CI ran on linux/amd64.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented, apart from a source comment that Reader is not concurrency-safe and the buffer must not change while being read. Writer has no locking; the README takes a Writer from a sync.Pool for each encode.

gotchas: Open issue #102 (Dec 2023, no reply): the Go generator treats offset 0 as 'allocate here', so a root inline struct whose first field is another inline struct is allocated twice and decodes as zeros. The reporter's workaround is a dummy leading field.

Failures are silent. An out-of-bounds offset makes a Viewer point at a zeroed sentinel array, ReadAsRoot returns no error, and strings or arrays longer than their [<N] bound are truncated to N on read.

Viewer strings and slices alias the input buffer (zero-copy), so reusing or overwriting that buffer changes values you already hold. Without @packed(true), padding bytes are not cleared and can leak earlier buffer or system memory (README).

C runtime (c/karmem.h): the growable KarmemWriter calls realloc() with the requested total but records capacity as max(2x old, total), so later allocations can write past the heap block. The fixed writer, which the benchmark uses, avoids this. The runtime functions and the generated _Null array are non-static definitions in headers, so include them from only one translation unit.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Karmem only for the job it was built for: a TinyGo/Go WASM module sharing one buffer with Zig, C, AssemblyScript or Odin code. For Go-only messaging, greenpack or ZebraPack are the catalogued Go options. For C++, YaFF (listed at ~2-2.5x faster flat reads than FlatBuffers) or SBE fit better, since Karmem has no C++ generator.
verified_claims_summary: The project's own benchmark encodes and decodes 1,000 monsters, each with a 100-element Vec3 path, on an Apple M1; toolchain versions are not stated, and FlatBuffers Go is v2.0.6. Natively, Karmem was ~5x faster to encode, ~18x faster to decode through the object API and ~9x faster to sum the paths with zero-copy readers (1.44 ms -> 0.16 ms); under TinyGo WASM on wazero the ratios were ~4.3x, ~27x and ~7.7x. The baseline is FlatBuffers' allocation-heavy Go object API (110k allocs/op on decode) with a similar but not identical schema, and no C++ implementation of either format was measured.
status_note: Abandoned: last code change Sep 2022, last commit (a wazero bump) Mar 2023, latest tag v1.2.9 (Aug 2022), and a data-corruption report sits unanswered. It is BSD-3-Clause and the Go runtime is ~135 lines on the stdlib only, so vendoring it with the generated code is practical, but you inherit the generator's bugs.
